one_liner: Header-only C++ image resizers: AVIR, quality-first sinc resampling, plus LANCIR, a SIMD Lanczos-3. No speed comparison against other libraries exists.
what_it_does: Resizes 1-4 channel interleaved raw buffers (uint8, uint16, float, double) up or down by any factor, and can do sub-pixel shifts. AVIR (avir::CImageResizer<>, avir.h) 2x-upsamples, interpolates with a bank of Peaked-Cosine-windowed sinc fractional-delay filters, then applies a correction filter; optional sRGB gamma, error-diffusion dither and several parameter sets (default, LR/ULR low-ringing, Low/High/Ultra). LANCIR (avir::CLancIR, lancir.h, self-contained) is a separable Lanczos resizer (a=3 by default) with a similar call shape: resizeImage(src, w, h, dst, nw, nh, channels, &params).
how_it_is_fast: LANCIR precomputes a filter bank at 1000 fractional offsets (enough for its 8-bit precision), replicates taps per channel to fit SIMD width, and runs the multiply-accumulate loops with SSE2, AVX, NEON or WASM SIMD128 intrinsics chosen at compile time. It resizes vertically first in batches of output rows sized to a roughly 5.5 MB cache budget, then horizontally per row, and keeps its buffers between calls so batches of same-sized frames skip reallocation and filter regeneration. AVIR relies mostly on compiler auto-vectorization of plain float code, with optional SSE float4 and de-interleaved AVX float8 types; the README says the AVX de-interleaved path gives up to 50% over non-SIMD code for 1-2 channel images.
when_to_use: You want a dependency-free, header-only C++ resizer you can vendor (MIT), with an 8-bit Lanczos-3 path that has NEON and WASM SIMD128 kernels as well as SSE2/AVX.
Batch-resizing many same-sized frames (video pipelines, asset baking): one CLancIR object per thread reuses its filters and buffers between calls.
Quality-critical downscaling or upscaling of photos where frequency response and low ringing matter more than time: AVIR's sinc and Peaked Cosine design, with selectable low-ringing parameter sets.
16-bit or float pipelines that need high-precision resampling (AVIR), accepting that it is slower than LANCIR.
Fractional-offset sub-pixel shifts or non-uniform x/y scale factors (kx, ky, ox, oy parameters).
when_not_to_use: Choosing the fastest CPU resizer: the repo has no timing against stb_image_resize2, OpenCV, libvips, Pillow-SIMD or IPP, and issue #18 (2020) says of AVIR 'I just tried to use it for real-time processing and, well, it's not fast'. Benchmark against fast_image_resize or zimg first.
16-bit-accurate fast resizing: LANCIR accepts uint16 and float buffers, but its precision is limited to 8-bit.
Built-in parallelism: neither resizer threads by default. AVIR needs your own CImageResizerThreadPool implementation, and LANCIR offers no slicing helper.
Rotation, affine warps or EWA/radial filtering: only orthogonal (separable) resizing is provided, and the README warns about diagonal aliasing.
One binary that adapts to the CPU: LANCIR picks SSE2, AVX or NEON from compiler macros, so a default x86-64 build gets SSE2 only unless you compile with AVX enabled.

integration.min_toolchain: C++98 (both headers carry pre-C++11 fallbacks for nullptr and cstdint); tested with GCC, MSVC, Clang and Intel C++
integration.platforms: any CPU with IEEE float; LANCIR SIMD on x86 SSE2/AVX, ARM NEON (32- and 64-bit), WASM SIMD128, scalar elsewhere; AVIR optional SSE (avir_float4_sse.h) and AVX (avir_float8_avx.h) types
integration.thread_safety: AVIR CImageResizer is documented as thread-safe: one object can serve concurrent resizes, but splitting a single image across threads needs your own CImageResizerThreadPool. CLancIR is not thread-safe because it reuses internal buffers, so use one object per thread.

gotchas: Floating-point output is not clamped in either resizer, so sinc and Lanczos overshoot can leave values outside [0,1]. Issue #12 reported green and pink pixels when resizing float buffers while uint8 was fine. Clamp before converting.

AVIR at k=1 is not an identity copy: it always low-pass filters first and applies a correction filter at the end. Its default parameters may change between releases, so save the parameter set if you need reproducible output.
AVIR's sRGB gamma correction is off by default, and when enabled it also applies to alpha unless Vars.AlphaIndex is set. The README warns it can produce 'greenish/reddish/bluish haze' near edges.

Version 3.1 removed the scanline 'unbiasing' added in 2.8, which the author now calls a compiler-dependent statistical error, and fixed a 16-bit to 8-bit conversion bug. Output from 2.x and 3.1 differs.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick LANCIR over stb_image_resize2-based siblings (stb-image-resize-opt, tir) when you need a C++ header with NEON and WASM SIMD Lanczos kernels and will measure speed yourself, and pick AVIR when resampling quality matters more than time. For documented speed wins, zimg (Lanczos about 2x faster than FFmpeg swscale) and fast_image_resize (faster than libvips) have measured numbers that this entry lacks.
verified_claims_summary: Nothing is compared against another resizer. The README times only AVIR itself (245 ms single-threaded, 74 ms with 8 threads, for an 8-bit RGB 5184x3456 to 1920x1280 downscale on an i7-7700K, Intel C++ 18.2 with AVX2, harness not published) and calls LANCIR 'up to three times faster' than AVIR with no numbers. The README's comparison plots are quality-only (frequency response and dynamic range), and their 'Lanczos-3' is the project's own CLancIR per other/frtest.cpp.
status_note: Maintained by its single author (AVIR 3.1, LANCIR 3.1.1, last commit 2026-08-22, no open issues or PRs), MIT-licensed, header-only with no dependencies, so easy to vendor; the README asks for the credit line 'AVIR image resizing algorithm designed by Aleksey Vaneev'.
measurement_notes: Code read this session: no timing code exists in the repo. other/frtest.cpp is a quality test only: it includes a private header (../../../../libvox/Sources/Core/CWorkerThreadPool.h), so it does not build from the public repo, and its Lanczos-3 baseline is CLancIR itself (the IS_AVIR=0 branch). bin/ holds only prebuilt imageresize binaries (linux-x64, win32, win64); issue #26 asks for their sources, and none are published in the repo. The README does not say which AVIR version produced the 245/74 ms figures; they name Intel C++ 18.2, a 2018 toolchain, and predate the 3.0 change that the changelog says sped up upsizing by 10-25%. The quality plots are labelled AVIR 2.9, built with the 2.8 'unbiasing' that 3.1 removed as a statistical error, so they may not match 3.1 output. No correctness bug behind any speed number was found, because no comparative speed number exists. Tier D stands.
